newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM sees no short-term inflation remedy.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM sees no short-term inflation remedy.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus says he does not expect any dramatic changes soon in the country's battle against stubborn consumer inflation.
"I do not expect inflation, which is somewhere around eight-and-something percent, to suddenly veer in any direction," Klaus said on Czech television on Sunday.
The government had forecast eight percent inflation for the whole of 1996, but higher-than-expected domestic demand has kept annual consumer price growth stubbornly high.
"I would rather see it suddenly veer downwards, but I don't forecast that in the short-term," said Klaus.
The central bank undertook measures to tighten money supply growth in June, and inflationary growth slowed to 8.9 percent year-on-year in September.

The 55-year-old prime minister, amid growing opposition pressures to act quickly over record trade deficits, reiterated that his government was not preparing measures that would radically affect the currency rate of the Czech crown.
"We do not expect, there does not threaten, and we are not preparing any shift (in the exchange rate)," Klaus told the television audience.

Some economists have suggested a devaluation of the Czech crown to boost exports in the face of a ballooning 100 billion crown trade deficit, a measure repeatedly ruled out by Klaus' government and the central bank.
The official Czech Statistical Bureau reported that exports had grown 6.4 percent in nominal terms while imports grew a nominal 15.2 percent during the first eight months of the year.
